newsitem.title: USA: Miami woes not affecting tourism, Dade mayor says.
newsitem.headline: Miami woes not affecting tourism, Dade mayor says.

text.p: The mayor of Florida's Dade County sought to reassure potential visitors Thursday that Miami's financial ills have not affected the larger metropolitan area or its beaches, airport, seaport and tourism-dependent economy.

"I'm very concerned with the national and international headlines. For the national and international community, there is no difference between Miami and Miami Beach and Dade County," county Mayor Alex Penelas said. "The city of Miami is our flagship city and we all suffer from the consequences."
Miami is the Dade County seat but is only one of 29 independent municipalities in the sprawling urban mishmash generally referred to as "Miami."
The city has a $68 million deficit for the year that began Oct 1, and suffered the ignominy on Tuesday of having the governor put it under guardianship of state advisors.

Penelas called a news conference to announce that the county would aid the city by continuing to offer the $10 million loan it first offered in October, and by offering to buy some prime, city-owned waterfront land targeted for a new basketball arena.
The mayor said the county, which has already loaned a dozen budget executives to the city, was prepared to provide police and other services if the city is forced to cut back.

Penelas also said he would appoint a commission of government, business and community leaders to draft a contingency plan to provide all public services to Miami if the city is dissolved "either by vote or through complete financial collapse."

"I am not, repeat I am not, in favor of abolishing our signature city of Miami," Penelas said. "We stand committed to help the city of Miami through its problems. This financial crisis is serious but it is also managable."

But Penelas also expressed concern that Miami's fiscal disgrace would deter visitors, crippling the county's $8.5 billion tourism industry. Work crews are already building bleachers for one of the area's biggest tourism events, the New Year's Day Orange Bowl celebration.

Penelas stressed that Miami accounts for only 2 percent of the county's acerage and 17 percent of its population. Miami International Airport, the Port of Miami, the public hospital and the tourist police program are all run by the county and are all unaffected by Miami's budget crunch, he said.
"Dade County's fiscal position continues to be strong and healthy," Penelas said.
Tourism and business officials said so far, Miami's woes have not hurt the area's economy.
"Businesses are continuing to look at Miami as a viable location for their headquarters," Carol Wyllie, head of the Beacon Council economic development group, said.
An official with the Greater Miami Visitors & Convention Bureau, Robert Beatty, said, "1996 was a banner year for the tourism industry. Even with these problems we expect 1997 to be even better."

Nor has Dade County's credit rating been affected. While Miami's credit rating has been cut to non-investment grade, or "junk" status, the county's general obligation debt is rated A-1 by Moody's Investor Service and A-plus by Standard & Poor's Corp.
The ratings signify "strong capacity to pay interest and repay principle," and "upper-medium grade obligations."

The county is set to price a $120 million solid waste bond issue next week, but has received assurances from financial advisers that "the rating agencies and the investors are aware of the difference" between Dade County and Miami, assistant county manager David Morris said.
"We think we'll get the same good prices as we always do," he said.
